Today at noon at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Waitman T. Menear on Madison street, the marriage of their daughter, Miss Ada Yell Menear to Mr. Harry Anglim Williamson was solemnized in the presence of the relatives and near friends of the bride and groom.

The parlor where the marriage ceremony was performed was artistically decorated in ferns and clover blossoms. On the mantle piece was laid a profusion of pink clovers massed with ferns and the bay window where the couple stood during the ceremony was transformed into a bow of beauty by the use of the flowers and ferns.

The bride was becomingly attired in a gown of soft white satin and carried lilies of the valley. Her going away gown was of blue rajah silk.

A luncheon was served in the dining room which was tastefully decorated in profusion of wisteria blossoms and ferns. A basket of wisteria formed the center piece of the serving table over which a battenberg cloth was spread over green. Assisting in the dining room were Misses Edna Menear, Mary and Anna Russell, Lenore Braham, and Bess Mason. Mrs. J. N. Black received the guests on their arrival.

When the bride's cake was cut, the ring was discovered by Miss Bessie Arnett, the money by Miss Edna Menear, the needle fell to Miss Mary Russell and the thimble to Miss Engle. Miss Lenore Braham caught the bride's bouquet.

Mr. and Mrs. Williamson left on a two weeks trip to parts unknown.

WASHINGTON, July 22.--The fuel testing plant of the United States Geological Survey, at Denver, Col., one of the factors in the conservation of the coal supply of the country, will resume operations the latter part of July. At this plant the government is endeavoring to obtain greater efficiency from the coals of the Rocky mountain fields by washing and cooking them. Many of the coals of the West contain such quantities of impurities—ash and sulphur—that they are not of much value for commercial use. It has been the government's purpose to wash the impurities out of these coals so that they can be utilized. The success already obtained warrants a continuation of this work. During the last fiscal year, ninety tests of coals were made at the Denver plant, resulting in many of them being decidedly improved.

Of thirty-seven Western coals tested at the Denver plant, all but three produced good coke though many of them considered as non-coking. The importance of this is seen when the immensity of the smelting business of the West is realized and the therefore enormous demand for good coke. Several of these coals without washing have failed to make coke fit for metallurgical purposes owing to the large amount of sulphur in them. Other coals would not even make steam without washing process.

It is likely that the final results of these tests will add millions of dollars to the fuel values of the West. It has already been shown that many of coals that in the past have not been mined because of their impurities can now be profitably utilized. This will extend the life of the fuel supply and make possible vast industrial enterprises in the West that would not locate there had the government not taken this step.

The lack of knowledge of the nature of the coals of the West has been its chief handicap to commercial development. With the finest supply of bituminous and anthracite coal in the world located in the Eastern part of the country, it has been felt that the West, in some instances, could not compete in manufacturing. The results shown by the government have done much to dispel this idea and the West has been going forward at a rapid rate. Still further developments are expected upon the compilation of the tests this year. The Denver plant is in charge of A. W. Belden, assisted by C. R. Delamater. A bulletin will soon be issued by the geological survey on the work already accomplished at this plant.

A young woman, with more than the ordinary share of good looks, finely groomed and gowned in the latest mode, got on a street car at Bedford and Division-avcs. She followed their glances and on one of the topmost branches, at least 20 feet from the ground, she saw a shivering gray cat.

"Please tell me how long that poor little thing has been there," the young woman said to a boy.

"Well, I'm on my way home from school now, and when I passed here this morning I saw a dog chase it up there," answered the youngster. "We have thrown sticks and things to get it down, but it's no use."

Maj. Davis finally found silent moment. He shouted to the boat which was spinning round and round under the influence of its crew, which was rowing regardless of time or correct form. He ordered it to pull up alongside the wharf and stay there.


"Aye, aye, sir!" called back the first sergeant in command of the rudder, and immediately headed for the channel, and did not stop until he was nearly out of sight of the wharf.


Other boats were loaded also. When one man was told to take a position in the bow and stand up with a boat hook in his hand, he promptly climbed into the stern and sat down.


Another man got his boat loaded and began to shout a lot of orders about "port" and "starboard" and "helm." His crew, however, having no conception of any nautical subject whatsoever, continued to row every man for himself and managed to get a nice violent up and down motion of the oars which looked fine, but which did not move the boat from its original position.

Oarsmen who had caught on to the fact that a long pull and a strong pull and pull all together is the thing after all, could not be restrained. The man who was instructed to stand in the boat with a boat hook in hand and lean out of something on the wharf, one man, in his effort to obey instructions, hooked Maj. Davis about the legs.


However, when the officers' voices were tired and they refrained from giving orders, the boat practice went along smoothly enough. Last night's use of the flotilla justified the morning's work.

To the Editor of the Kick Column

I do not wish to write heatedly or ill-advisedly, but I feel sure of my ground when I enter the strongest sort of protest possible against the conduct of certain of the student element at the theaters in New Haven. The duty of the Hyperion is well defined. They must see to it that there are less "coppers" in the audience and more "coppers" in the aisles. By the former I mean the pennies which are thrown on the stage at the most inopportune moments by certain students, who, in some manner believe they are exceedingly funny whereas a fact, they lack even the most fundamental elements of gentlemanliness. By the latter I refer to the police.

I am aware that the theater management has done its best to free its audiences from these objectionable practices. Paragraphs have been inserted in the programs, calling the attention of all to the fact that those who throw missiles of any kind on the stage will be subject to ejection, arrest and prosecution. That paragraph should be more strictly enforced, especially as regards the dramas. A penny or two dropped while chorus girls are having their fling is not nearly such a serious matter as during such splendidly acted scenes as were presented here Saturday in "The Witching Hour" after which Mr. Mason felt called upon in a curtain speech to make mention of the coins which had fallen.

Our student element calls itself gentlemanly. I believe it is so in most things. But he only is a gentleman who is a gentleman all the time. The students must have enough education to realize that they would not make such asses of themselves at the theaters in their home towns; why should they in New Haven to the discomfort of all about them, who have paid their good money to witness an excellent performance? There is also the physical danger to be considered. One of the actresses here lately was hit by one of these falling pennies and was cut on the hand. Suppose it had hit her in the eye.

Professor Phelps is a good student of the drama. He has aroused true appreciation of the goodies of the stage with any number of Yale men past and present. Is it not possible for him to give his young friends some worthwhile suggestions as to how to act when witnessing performances of real merit. The time has come for a change.

The statement made in this correspondence yesterday to the effect that the insurance company was "revoked" on refusal to allow examination by the insurance commissioner of the state and an actuary of his choosing, was an error, because of misunderstanding of what Commissioner of Insurance Julian said and the substitution of the word "revoked" for "suspended." Los ANGELES, Cal., APRIL 6 --
After a week's stay at the ports
of Los Angeles, during which time
elaborate and almost continuous
entertainment has been lavished
upon the officers and men, the Atlantic battleship fleet sailed this
morning for Santa Barbara.


The departure of the big ships
was preceded by spectacular evolu-
tions in the bay—Santa Monica—
lasting more than an hour, which
were witnessed by immense crowds,
fully equaling in numbers the mul-
titude of people that welcomed the
fleet at San Pedro last Saturday.
The movement of the fighting ships
began at 8 o'clock; at that hour
the first division, the Connecticut,
Kansas, Vermont and Louisiana,
steamed out of San Pedro harbor
and was joined by the second di-
vision from Long Beach.


Simultaneously with the start of
the first and second divisions, the
third division, the Minnesota, Ohio,
Missouri and Maine weighed anchor
and left Venice to join the fourth
division, the Illinois, Mississippi,
Kentucky and Alabama at Redondo.


The reunited fleet then steamed
up the coast past Playa del Rey,
Venice, Ocean Park and Santa
Monica, making two complete
swings around the bay and offer-
ing a most magnificent marine
pageant.


At the conclusion of the maneu-
vers, the ships, with flying colors
and cheers by the blue Jackets that
lined their sides, bid farewell to
their generous hosts and at 11
o'clock stood out to sea for Santa
Barbara, which is expected to be
reached at 4 o'clock this afternoon.

ing. To make yourself at all heard
you must shout into the ear of a COM-
panion. So intense is the strain, says
writer In St. Nicholas, that you mar-
vel how day in and day out human
ears can withstand the ordeal.

You find yourself inside what seems
an enormous steel cigar painted a neat
pearl gray, a color which is serviceable
and does not dazzle the eye. Light
comes TO you partly through portholes
and in part from incandescent lamps
placed fore and aft in the darker parts
of the hull.

You have expected, OF course, to
land in a tangle OF whirling machinery
that fills the inside Of the boat from
stem to stern, threatening with every
revolution to take an arm or a leg off.
Instead the first thing you see Is an
uninterrupted working space or
deck, measuring by 8 or 10 feet.

At the stern, far in the background,
are the machines and engines. In fact,
this section of the vessel Is nothing but
machinery, a rumbling mass Of silvery
steel and glittering brass revolving at
the rate OF 800 times a minute, so com-
pact that you wonder how the various
parts can turn without conflicting or
how It is possible for human hands to
squeeze through the maze to oil the
machinery.

But this economy OF space Is as moth-
ing TO what you will see. The floor
you stand on is cover for the cells of
the storage batteries wherein Is pent
up the electricity with which your boat
will propel herself when she runs sub-
merged. The walls amidships and the
space in the bow are gigantic ballast
tanks TO be filled with water that will
[provide buoyancy].

The four torpedoes, measuring six-
teen feet three inches long, eighteen
inches In diameter and weighing 1900
pounds each, are lashed end for end in
pairs at either side, and directly over
these are tool boxes and hinged bunks
for the crew TO sleep in.

The very air which is taken along to
keep life in you in case the boat should
be detained beneath the surface longer
than usual is compressed in a steel cyl-
inder under 1000 pounds per square inch. A
pressure so intense that were the cyl-
inder TO spring a leak no larger than a
pin hole and were the tiny stream OF
escaping air to strike a human being it
would penetrate him through and
through and drill a hole through an
inch thick board behind him.

And yet everything about the inte-
rior arrangements OF this boat is so sim-
ple that you can see at a glance its
purpose. Away forward, where the
tip OF the cigar comes to a point, are
the two torpedo tubes out OF which
the gunner will send his deadly pro-
jectiles seething beneath the waters at
an unsuspecting hull.

Directly under the conning tower is
a platform, three feet square and ele-
vated three feet from the deck, upon
which the captain stands, head and
shoulders extending into the tower, so
that while at his post he is visible to
the crew only from the waist line
down, and at the feet Of the captain
and on level with his platform is
stationed another of the officers, in
charge Of the wheel that controls the
diving rudders and the gauges that
register the angle Of ascent and de-
cline and show how deep the boat is
down.

The two officers are in personal COM-
munication, so that In case of heart
disease or other mishap either can
jump to the other man's place.

The expectations of Mr. Defebaugh with respect to improve a condition after the first of the year are fully shared by those connected with the trade in this part of the country.

The town of Richton, on the Mobile Jackson and Kansas City road just south of Laurel promises to soon come to the front as one of the centers of the lumber trade of this part of the country. It already has four or five mills of no small capacity, all cutting on full time, and travelling men rank Richton right up with the magic city of Bogalusa, La., as an example of the commercial potentialities of the lumber business when concentrated at one point, with the difference in favor of Richton that while Bogalusa has but one large mill upon which to depend for sustenance, Richton has several independent establishments that insure the prosperity of the place for long time to come. But now Richton is to have another big mill that will rank along with the largest in this part of the world. It will be put in by Bentley and Emery, who come from Pennsylvania, the home of many of the most successful lumber operators of the south. They are experienced in the sawmilling business and have been successful wherever they have operated. Their Richton plant will have capacity of 150,000 feet per day and will employ some 250 hands.

At the December sitting of the chancery court at Waynesboro, Miss., a decree was entered empowering E. F. Ballard, receiver of the West-King Lumber company, to advertise and sell the property for the benefit of creditors, and an inventory of the property is now being taken and the sale will take place the first Monday in February. The mill owes the old bank of Waynesboro about $75,000, and it was this debt that caused the suspension of the bank last June, and necessitated the bank, in order to reopen, to issue certificates of deposit to depositors for their balances due, based upon collecting this West-King debt, the bank later closing permanently as the result of second run being made upon it; and since then matters have been in a tangle of litigation, the last court having now come to the rescue by ordering the sale of the mill property.

The total debt hanging over the mill is something like $375,000, but it is claimed that the value of the property is something like a million dollars. The outstanding certificates of deposit of the defunct bank amount to about the mills total indebtedness to that institution, and are about the only deposits the bank has. Depositors hope that sale for sum near the real value of the plant will be made.

The Hines tracts extend, with interruptions, all the way from the gulf coast on up to Poplarville and Lamar county and on west to where the Goodyear holding begin. With the death of Judge Scott, as he was affectionately called by the whole county, another landmark of this old town passes away. There has probably never been a lawyer who has practiced at this bar within the last thirty years who in the examination of title to real estate when the records failed to show the chain of title, but has gone to the Judge for help; and it was seldom that he failed to put him on the right track.


Judge Scott passed his whole life here in Kingstree and loved his home and people with the intensity and zeal for which is noted the sturdy Scotch ancestry from which he sprung. strenuous work of the past two months
on the Flathead reservation in rounding
up and corralling the 50 bison of

Canadian government, has come to
naught and there will be no shipment

the animals were driven and it was
over this almost perpendicular cliff
that the herd escaped.


Next summer another attempt will
probably be made to round up the
bison.

Meinung richtig," fragt er, "da un-

fanden?" Er hält es deshalb nicht für
zutreffend, weil die Natur nicht mit

wohl zutreffend sein, aber dieser
Gedanke wird schwierig einen
Leser überzeugen, zumal denn er sich
vergegenwärtigt, daß die heutigen

geworden sind. So ist

durchbrochen und mit franckhaft ge-

Nur ist Claude, die Klatsch, eben-

New Orleans, La., Aug. 21.—Planters in Louisiana and Mississippi have become intensely alarmed over the rapidity of the boll weevil spread &c. the eastward, on account of the ravages of the boll weevil in Avoyelles Parish, this state. Cotton farmers have been compelled to plow up their fields and replant them in sugar cane this season. This news was brought to the city today by W. A. White, a planter of Woodside, fully forty farmers in his neighborhood having been compelled to quit planting cotton altogether on account of the weevil.

Curious among vegetable growths
and one which is seldom seen of men
Is the rootless cactus of the California
desert, says the Technical World.
This plant, round, compact growth,
rolls about the level floor of the des-
ert for some eight or nine months of
the year, tossed hither and yon by
the winds which blow with fierceness
over all of California's sand plat dur.
ing those months.


At the coming of the rains, or
rather the cloudbursts, which sweep
the desert in it's springtime, this cac-
tus takes root wherever it happens to
have been dropped by the last wind
OF which it was the plaything and i'm
mediately begins to put out all around
1t small shoots, which in turn become
cacti, exactly like the parent plant.


These young growths increase in
size rapidly, sucking the moisture
both from the parent plant and from
the surrounding earth. The roots do
not penetrate the soil deeply, but
spread often over a circle whose
radius is not less than ten feet. These
roots, too, are small, but practically
innumerable, and they get every bit
of moisture and plant food to be had
In the territory they cover.

Correspondence to The Bulletin:
Springfield, Ill., Jan. 20.—At the
time this letter is written (Monday)
There is strong probability that a
primary election bill will pass both
houses before the end of the week.
There will be some disappointment to
the part of advocates of a direct plurality
primary law; for this bill is not
that kind of measure, except in a
limited sense. Comity officers are to
be terminated by a direct plurality
vote—a measure not contained in the
law of 1900, which is the basis for the
new bill. But all other nominations
are to be made by convention substantially in the manner provided by
the old law. The state is to be divided into delegate districts—the dist.
this year is to be the same as in
1906 and hereafter is to be fixed by the
party central committee of each
party. The later provision is taken
from the old law but constitutional
objections are avoided by providing
that the county committeeman shall
be elected at the primaries, thus making them election officers under the
law.

The new measure contains one provision that distinguishes it vitally
from the old law. There are to be
two ballots at the primaries—one a
delegate ballot and the other candidate ballot. The plurality principle
prevails in the naming of delegates
and in their instruction. The candidate for office receiving the highest
number of votes in any delegate district is given the delegates from that
district, but the delegates, instead of being instructed for one ballot only, are
bound by their instructions until released by the candidates in open convention. The effect of this provision
is likely to be far reaching. It will
mean many deadlocked conventions,
but on the whole is received with satisfaction as an improvement over the
"one ballot" instructions provided in
the old law.

The new measure, which is the product of the joint conference committee, is a compromise, and as stated
is not satisfactory to the direct plurality advocates; but there is a tendency to accept it on the ground that
no other measure can be passed at
this time, and in the hope that it may
be amended at the next session of the
legislature if serious defects appear
in the primary system which it provides. Many members would like to
pass two bills—one the Oglesby direct
plurality bill, the other a convention
bill; like the committee measure now.
Then let the people say
at the next general election which
kind of law they want. But there
are many difficulties in the way of
this plan, chief of which is that it
would leave the state without a primary law applicable to the campaign
this year.

Just how the new primary law will
meet the gubernatorial contest is not
yet clear. The chances are that it
will have the effect of bringing out
two or three candidates, whose plan
will be to divide up the state in such
way that no one of them will have
a majority of the state convention delegates and that a winning combination
may be effected in the convention. Politicians generally take the
view that any kind of a primary law
will help Gov. Deneen, though probably, he would fare better under a direct plurality law than he will under
the one now about to be enacted.

It is reported that James McNabb,
editor of the Carrollton Gazette, may
become candidate for the Democratic nomination for lieutenant governor. McNabb is a lawyer as well as
journalist, and is well known both
among newspaper men and among
lawyers. It is known that many Democrats in his district are urging him
to become a candidate.

ADOLPH NARRÉ

ished to hear faint cry from the in
side. There was somebody fastened
up in that living prison. He thought
it must be a tramp and hastily broke
the lead seal and threw back the door.


''Thank heaven,'' cried weak voice,
and there came tottering toward him
woman. Hanson took her in his
arms and lifted her to the ground. As
he held her thrill passed through
him. She opened her eyes and he
knew her. It was the girl that he had
met in Chicago, hundreds of miles
away, weeks before.


Her story was simple one. She
had been picknicking out near May
fair, northwest of Chicago, with a
party of friends, and while they were
waiting for a train they had engaged
in a game of hide and seek. She had
thoughtlessly hidden in an empty
freight car on siding. She crept
back into a corner of the car and
within a minute or two one of the
train crew came along and closed the
door and sealed it. Then switch
engine picked up the car and it was


made up into train and sent to the


northwest. Nobody had happened to


hear the cries of the girl imprisoned
on the inside, and she had been


carried to the arms of the man she
loved her.


It was fate. They both felt it. And


after Hanson had taken her to his
mother's house and had her cared for
tenderly he telegraphed to her parents
in Chicago, who had been searching


everywhere for a trace of her. He
told them that she was safe and well,
and in the hands of friends, and that
she was going to make visit to his
sister.


On the tenth of July they were
married. Chicago American.

have some of the strongest men in the

speakers campaign will be in charge
of General T. Coleman Dupont, of
Delaware, between whom and Mr.
Murphy especially friendly relations
exist.

Jerome Yields.

Mr. Jerome had previously elected to Mrs. Thaw detailing conversations she had with Thaw years prior to the tragedy, but Justice Bowling ruled that the declarations of the defendant's wife were admissible on general principles and without any reference to the Wood case, under which the evidence in dispute was admitted last year, and which Mr. Jerome had been expected to ask construction of this year.

"I will not except to your honor's ruling," said the district attorney, as he took his seat, after his objection, for the state has no power of appeal. Then Mr. Jerome attacked the witness in another way and by standing immediately in front of her and objecting to practically every question which Mr. Littleton asked in his preliminary examination as to her early history, cut the young woman's recital from the effective narrative form it assumed last year into a hundred fragments. Many of the objections based upon irrelevancy and immateriality were sustained by the court. When these failed the prosecutor was ever ready with others until the testimony was practically torn into shreds and had lost entirely the many little touches of human interest which were a part of the narration last year when no objections were offered. Mr. Jerome said his objections were intended to cut out all stories about pet cats and lot of other stuff which had no place in the trial.

Good Progress Made.

The day however, was one of good progress for the defense. The elder Mrs. Thaw, pale and weak from her recent illness, was assisted to the witness chair and repeated large part of the testimony she gave a year ago. Her appearance and the sincerity of her evidence as she told of her son's strange conduct after meeting him, hearing her story, had marked effect on all who listened. On account of her weak condition her examination was interrupted by consent, to be resumed some time next week, when she will tell of Thaw's infancy.

District Attorney Jerome's manner while the mother was on the stand was all deference, and it was his suggestion which led to the respite in her ordeal. But when the young wife took the stand the change was marked. Jerome glared at her from the very first and his objections were fairly shouted in her ears. Not accustomed to court usage from her former experience, the young woman waited patiently for ruling to each objection. When they were sustained she was silent; when overruled she was ever ready with her response.

Thaw Irrational.

Effective testimony was given at the morning session by Miss Alice C. Fletcher of Washington, a long time friend of Thaw's and a frequent visitor at their home. She said she had known Harry Thaw for 26 years, and he had always impressed her as irrational.

Miss Catherine O'Neill, who nursed Thaw as a boy, from his third to his tenth year, added her evidence to that already adduced as to irrational conduct and tendencies on the part of the defendant. Two doormen at the police station where Thaw was confined the night of the tragedy, repeated their stories of last year of Thaw's irrational appearance and his complaining of noises that did not exist.

The trial may be concluded in two weeks more.

Miss Fletcher On Stand.

Miss Alice C. Fletcher of Washington, was at the Thaw household in Pittsburg, and had known Harry K. Thaw for 26 years, was the first witness today. She declared that Thaw was an unusual child—nervous.

The first of the discursive subjects at the Short Course Friday afternoon was the lecture of Dr. X. W. Thomas of Denver on the subject "Irrigating Institutions." At the outset of his address Dr. Thomas referred to a visit he made to Canon City in 1866. The town, then, he said, reminded him of Goldsmith's deserted village. The irrigation ditch, asserted Dr. Thomas, is the base upon which rests the agricultural structure of the entire semi-arid region.

Irrigation is almost as old as man and was traced back by the speaker to the valleys of the Euphrates and the Nile, the original homes of the human race. A great deal of semi-arid land in the southwestern part of the United States was irrigated in prehistoric times by means of storage reservoirs and ditch systems, which in their essential features have not been excelled by our present day engineers.

The first irrigation of any consequence by Anglo-Saxons in this country was done by the Mormons in Utah. The water rights from a single stream drawn upon by the Mormons for irrigation fifty years ago is now worth between two and three millions of dollars. The first irrigation in Colorado was done at Golden by H. W. Wall in 1860. The first apples grown in this state sold for twenty-five cents, and an old rattle trap of wagon in those days brought to town a load of strawberries which sold for one hundred and twenty-five dollars.

Approximately 100,000 acres of semi-arid land in the southwestern part of the United States is now under irrigation and the products which it yields are worth hundreds of millions of dollars every year. Colorado has the greatest area of land under irrigation, California coming next. In this state more than 500,000 is invested in irrigation enterprises and the amount is being rapidly increased. Many of our irrigation ditches are constructed for temporary use only. They must sooner or later be replaced by permanent systems—steel pipes, cement lined ditches, etc. The territory lying along the base of the Rocky Mountains is indeed good country and must always be in demand if brought under cultivation by people living in the less favored sections of the republic.

The storage reservoir is the natural and inevitable complement of the ditch system of irrigation. The history, achievements and ambitions of the government reclamation service and the road work done were told, and from it the speaker said much was expected.

Dr. Thomas explained the Kansas-Colorado water suit, pointing out that it had its origin in the Wichita, Kansas real estate boom of a decade or so ago. The speaker referred to the connection of Clyde C. Dawson of this city with the Kansas-Colorado litigation, paying him a very high compliment on account of the value of his services to this state. He said, now and ever, that to Prof. Carpenter, more than anybody else, was the triumph of Colorado due. Capt. B. F. Hockaday was also eulogized in connection with this famous litigation as it was through him that Prof. Carpenter's services to the state were made available.

"Selecting and Handling the Dairy Cow" by O. C. Grigg of Minnesota was the next subject considered by the Short Course students. The ideal dairy cow is characterized by the following points:

San Francisco, Nov. 27.—Stanley Ketchel of Grand Rapids, Mich., regained the middleweight championship of the world yesterday and reversed his defeat of last September when he sent Billy Papke, the Illinois "thunderbolt," crashing to the floor before a well directed blow that caught his opponent flush upon the chin. The end came in the eleventh round, prior to which Ketchel showed clearly that he was master of his opponent at any kind of fighting. Round by round, Ketchel forced his opponent and when opportunity offered, planted his right to head or body generally escaping without damaging return.

Belying his appearance and forcing the fight throughout every minute, Ketchel was stronger up to the moment of the knockout blow than was his opponent.

Ketchel was victor throughout. His appearance during the early rounds did not tend to encourage those who had backed him at odds of 10 to 10 and 10 to 9.

In the first round Ketchel drove Papke into a neutral corner, landing right and left almost at will, and thereafter the Illinois contender was always at a disadvantage.

It was in the seventh that Ketchel used his right to the greatest advantage. From this time on the crowd awaited the knockout punch that Ketchel was apparently withholding. In the ninth Papke was sent reeling across the ring and nearly went to his knees by a powerful blow delivered in a clinch. He arose to meet Ketchel's right, which twice landed on the jaw. Papke went to his corner, bleeding freely from the nose. This was the beginning of the end. In the following round Papke twice turned his back on Ketchel's swift assaults and deliberately ran away.

In the eleventh and final round Ketchel was as fresh and strong as at any time during the fight. He tapped Papke lightly on the jaw and then rushed him halfway across the ring, planting two hard rights to the stomach. A moment later as they broke out of a clinch, Ketchel swung the left at three-quarters length, landing squarely on the point of the chin. Papke struck at full length, his head rapping the floor with terrible force. He had just enough strength to regain his feet, and while he crouched in an attitude half protected, Ketchel sent his right to the head four times in quick succession and almost pushed Papke over with a left hook. Papke fell forward on his knees, his hands supporting his head bowed in agony. Referee Jack Welsh counted eleven, as did also the time keeper, and then, advancing toward Ketchel, threw the Michigan fighter's glove aloft. Papke, still dazed, seemed not to realize his defeat.

Papke said after the fight: "I am not satisfied with the outcome. I want a return! I did not hear the count; I heard the referee say six, and then I stopped. I would have been able to continue the fight, as I was not hurt and recovering fast. I want a return match."

Ketchel said: "I anticipated this result long before I entered the ring and backed my opinion with my own money. Papke's victory in the South was an accident. Under proper conditions I am willing to fight him again."

We come now to the question of labor. One important phase of the policies of the present administration has been an anxiety to secure for the wage-earner an equality of opportunity and such positive statutory protection as shall place him on equal footing in dealing with his employer.


The Republican party has passed an employers liability act for interstate railroads, and has established an eight hour law for government employees and on government construction. The essence of the reform effected by the former, is the abolition of the fellow-servant rule and the introduction of the comparative negligence theory by which an employee injured in the service of his employer does not lose all his right to recover because of slight negligence on his part.


Then there is the act providing for compensation for injury to government employees, together with the various statutes requiring safety appliances upon interstate commerce railroads for the protection of their employees and limiting the hours of their employment.


These are all instances of the desire of the Republican party to do justice to the wage-earners.


Doubtless a more comprehensive measure for compensation of government employees will be adopted in the future; the principle in such cases has been recognized and in the necessarily somewhat slow course of legislation will be more fully embodied in definite statutes.


The interests of the employer and the employee never differ except when it comes to a division of the joint profit of labor and capital into dividends and wages. This must be a constant source of periodical discussion between the employer and the employee, as indeed are the other terms of the employment.


To give to employees their proper position in such controversy, to enable them to maintain themselves against employers having great capital, they may well unite, because in union there is strength, and without it, each individual laborer and employee would be helpless. The promotion of the industrial peace through the fundamentals of the trade agreement is often one of the results of such union when intelligently conducted.


There is a large body of laborers, however, skilled and unskilled, who are not organized into unions. Their rights before the law are exactly the same as those of the union men, and are to be protected with the same care and watchfulness.


In order to induce their employer into compliance with their request for changed terms of employment, workmen have the right to strike in a body.


They have a right to use such persuasion as they may, provided it does not reach the point of duress, to lead their reluctant co-laborers to join them in their union against their employer, and they have right, if they choose, to accumulate funds to support those engaged in strike, to delegate to officers the power to direct the action of the union, and to withdraw themselves and their associates from dealings with or giving custom to those with whom they are in controversy.

Dakota, having passed the Tenth Legis-

approval or rejection.

That section 40 of the constitution
of the state of North Dakota is amended
to read as follows:


Sec. 140. Amendment. RAILROAD cor
porations and common carriers required
to keep Office in the state and make re
ports.] Every railroad corporation and
common carrier organized in, or doing
business in this state, under the laws or
authority thereof, shall have and main
tain public office or place in the state
for the transaction of it's business where
a record of the transfers of it's stock
shall be made and in which shall be
kept for public inspection, books IN
which shall be recorded the amount of
capital stock subscribed and by whom,
the names of the owners Of the stock
and the amount owned by them respec-
lively, the amount of stock paid in and
by whom, and the transfers of said
stock; the amount of its assets and
liabilities and the names and place of
residence of it's officers. The directors
of every railroad corporation and of
every common carrier doing business in
this state shall annually make report,
under oath, to the auditor of public
accounts, or some officer or officers to be
designated by law, of all their acts and
doings,- which report shall include such
matters relating to railroads and com
mon carriers as may be prescribed by
law. Similar reports shall be made to
such other officers and at such times
and places as may be required by law
and the legislative assembly shall pass
laws enforcing by suitable penalties the
provisions of this section.

the pirate chief, who was on deck,
came down into the cabin and seeing
the father of the unlucky young man
lamenting over his son's death, ad-
dressed the old man and condoled
with him on his son's unfortunate and
'undeserved' death. The chief finally
brought out of his pocket a roll of
$50 and handed the sum to the old
man as solatium.

NEW YORK, Sept. 23.-Alarm Is felt
In many sections of the State because
Of the rapid and continual spread of
the big forest fire in the Adirondacks.
New fires are frequently reported and
there are hundreds of small fires that
may become dangerous. Probably TO-
900 men are fighting the fires, but the
flames have gotten so far beyond CON
troll that only a drenching rain will
stop them.


The most extensive fires are reported
in Warren. Saratoga and Essex coun-
ties. In some places there has been
practically no rain since the middle of
July.


Rivers. creeks. wells and springs have
run dry. A big fire Is reported at
North Hudson, Essex county. Fifty
thousand acres of forest land are re-
ported ablaze in the North Creek sec
tion. There are a humber Of fires
burning in the Blue mountains, while

twenty cars on board and tied up to
a tug started from Jersey City for the
dock at Ninth street.


One car contained thirty Texas
steers, nine cars were filled with coal
the property of the Scranton and Lehigh
Coal Company, and the ten re-
maining cars were loaded with barrel
slaves.


All went well till the float was with-
in 100 feet of its destination, when,
without warning, it began to sink. In-
stantly there was a panic among the
crew, and the steers locked in their
cars seemed to know instinctively they

ifully. The crew of the tug cut inly

mals made a rush for the deck just as
the water engulfed the float, and fifteen

the car, which was carried down with

Should the Game Be Protested?

To the patrons of baseball at Barton Landing I wish to address this much about Friday's game. There seems abundant good authority that Elrod properly scored in the 9th inning, on Leonard's drive past third base, because the hit was fair, and that, if the umpire had declared the hit as it actually was, the game belonged to Barton Landing, 5 to 4. Suppose that, in addition to this, the umpire, after the game did say that he had judged hastily, that he knew, moment after making his decision, that the hit was fair, and that the game rightfully belonged to Barton Landing (it is reported that he made these statements), suppose all this should prove true, still doubt the propriety of protesting the game. Every lover of baseball should accept certain things as of the very essence of the game this much at least. As game progresses the plays therein become part and parcel of the game; and the sum total of the game is made up of these plays, not always as one sees them nor even as they actually are, but as the umpire rules them. Any other theory would turn the finest game in the world into chaos. Umpires cannot always give perfect judgment any more than courts can. It is often impossible to perfectly judge hard drive past third or first base. I have no proof that Umpire Brown was other than honest in his decision. If it is fact that he knew his mistake an instant later, but would not change his decision, it is to his credit probably; at all events it does not change the result. The baseball result is the game as he ruled it up to the time that play ceased. Our team have but to scan the score of that game as tabulated and reported by Barton authority, and published in the Boston Globe of last Saturday, to be proud of their team. It shows an errorless support of their pitcher in free-hitting and fast game of 11 innings. That's state record for the season. The great majority of the 5000 people who watched the game with all absorbing interest for two hours will concede that the team that gave such magnificent support to Pitcher Connolly while almost every man up hammered him, was not inferior to any Vermont team of 1908. Let's accept the result gracefully, in sportsmanlike spirit, make no protests, and say to our Barton neighbors the courteous thing: that we do not consider it any disgrace to lose this game to the State Champions.

W. R. Aldrich.

There are two classes of votes that have heretofore gone almost solidly for the Republicans in many states, but which seem this year to be thoroughly disguised with the leaders of that party that they will be found on election day almost a unit in opposition A. These are the negro vote and the organized labor vote.

A. The negro vote. This vote is the controlling factor in many Republican districts. In New York it holds the balance of power in the district represented in Congress by Herbert Parsons. But the vote of organized labor is in greater importance, since that vote counts in almost every congressional district in the country, and has practically endorsed the program of legislation for which the Democrats, under the leadership of John Sharp Williams, battled in the House of Representatives against the wishes and purposes of Speaker Cannon and the Republican majority of that body.

This program was approved by labor throughout the country on Easter Sunday in mass meetings held for the purpose of outlining the policy to be pursued by its organizations in respect to legislation, and in all those assemblies the votes of workingmen enrolled in labor unions were pledged to candidates who should favor such demands.

Hence it is that Republican congressmen are unhappy and cross and peevish these days.

Es war nicht in der ersten

einfach sehr schön. Die

Danach, in der ersten Woche,
war es etwas anders.
Aber der Regen kam bald. In
der nächsten Woche war es wieder.

Die Sonne schien schön und warm,
und die Luft war frisch. Es war
der erste Tag, der so hell war.
In den letzten Tagen war es
perfekt. Es war in der letzten
Woche; es war etwas besser als
die vorherige Woche, die die
die bisher gewesen hatte, es war
ein wenig unruhig, weil mir
das, was ich wollte, fehlte, und
die Arbeit schwer war, und
weder ich noch jemand anderes. Es

Die Arbeit war schwer. Die Tage

Es war mit den Jahren geworden

Es begann mit, schwierig in

Name, der Gott der Gnade.
Ohne uns nicht zu helfen; die

Was hier in Maryland zu

Die Liebe der Großzügigkeit

war in dem etwas beruhigter. Die

zum Beispiel nach, aber alles war
ein Rätsel für sie, in einem
Zimmer war ein Bett, wohl das der
anderen einerin.

Es hatte nicht geholfen.

Alles war auch wunderbar;
so leben, etwas wir nicht nötig,
zu lehre es dann mit dem Zimmer
war, und machen der Großvater war,
um sich überlegt welche Schritte ich
gemacht zu tun habe.

Meine Angst, ob auch die Sorge
habe die Wege des Großvaters erst
gegangen ist und das unvorhergesehen
gesehen. Meine beiden sind nicht da,

Wenn jemand wollte auf der

richteten Berichte überlassen; aber die

blieb; ich musste noch Entschuldigung
machen, meine Bitte mit tragen zu,
bevor dem Bezirksrichter die
Beweise von meiner rechtlichen Ent-
scheidung zu machen.

So, noch etwas über den Richter.

Es wollte plötzlich in tiefer
Seelenverbindung eine Erinnerung
vor mir auf, ich habe schon vor
mir, wie er von seinem Sinne
berichtet, unter der es nieder-
ging auf dem Kopf, ein wenig
wie er sich zusammenzog, als
er mich erblickte, als er sich dann in
das Gebet einfügte. Von einem
